chem_edx.0.0.summary: Every equation you write in GCSE Chemistry depends on getting formulae right, so this point underpins both papers. You need to recall the symbols and formulae of common elements (including the seven diatomic elements), the formulae of simple covalent and ionic compounds, and the charges of simple and compound ions. The big skill is working out the formula of any ionic compound by making the total positive charge equal the total negative charge, using brackets correctly for compound ions.

core.h: What a chemical formula tells you
core.p: A **chemical formula** uses element symbols and subscript numbers to show which elements are in a substance and how many atoms of each are combined. The subscript applies only to the symbol (or bracket) immediately in front of it. A large number written in front of a formula is not part of the formula: it tells you how many units (molecules or formula units) there are.
bullets: H₂O: 2 hydrogen atoms bonded to 1 oxygen atom in **one molecule** of water.
CO₂: 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms; the 2 belongs only to O.
3H₂O means **three molecules** of water: 6 H atoms and 3 O atoms in total.
Ca(OH)₂: the 2 multiplies everything inside the bracket, so 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H.
A symbol with no subscript means 1 atom (we never write a 1).
Every symbol starts with a capital letter; any second letter is lower case: Co is cobalt, but CO is carbon monoxide.

callouts.p: A chemical formula shows the symbols of the elements present in a substance and the number of atoms of each element in one unit of that substance.
CO (carbon monoxide, a compound) and Co (cobalt, an element) are completely different. Examiners do not award marks for wrong case.

core.h: Formulae of elements
core.p: Most elements are written simply as their symbol. **Metals** are giant structures, so the formula is just the symbol (Na, Fe, Cu, Mg). **Noble gases** exist as single atoms (He, Ne, Ar) because their outer shells are full and they do not need to bond. Carbon (as diamond or graphite) and silicon are giant covalent structures, so they are also written as C and Si.
bullets: Metals: Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al, Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Pb, Au.
Noble gases (monatomic): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe.
Giant covalent non-metals: C (diamond, graphite), Si.
Sulfur is usually written S and phosphorus P in GCSE equations.
Some non-metals exist as **simple molecules** and must be written with a subscript (see next section).

core.h: The seven diatomic elements
core.p: Seven elements exist as **diatomic molecules**, made of two atoms joined by a covalent bond. A single atom of these elements has an incomplete outer shell, so two atoms share electrons to become more stable. Whenever one of these elements appears in an equation as the element itself, you must write it with a subscript 2.
bullets: **H₂** hydrogen, **N₂** nitrogen, **O₂** oxygen.
**F₂** fluorine, **Cl₂** chlorine, **Br₂** bromine, **I₂** iodine (all the halogens in group 7).
Memory hook: 'Have No Fear Of Ice Cold Beer' (H, N, F, O, I, Cl, Br).
Only write them as X₂ when they are the free element: in compounds they follow normal rules (HCl, NaCl, H₂O).
Ozone O₃ exists but is not needed for this point.

callouts.p: In an equation such as 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, writing Cl on the left loses the formula mark and makes balancing impossible.

core.h: Formulae of common simple compounds to learn
core.p: Some formulae come up so often that you must know them by heart rather than work them out. Many are **simple covalent molecules** made of non-metals; others are common acids and ionic compounds used throughout the course.
bullets: Water H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, carbon monoxide CO.
Ammonia NH₃, methane CH₄, hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂.
Hydrochloric acid HCl, sulfuric acid H₂SO₄, nitric acid HNO₃.
Sodium hydroxide NaOH, calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂ (limewater).
Sodium chloride NaCl, calcium carbonate CaCO₃, copper(II) sulfate CuSO₄.
Sulfur dioxide SO₂, nitrogen dioxide NO₂ (pollutant gases).
Covalent compound names often use prefixes: **mono** = 1, **di** = 2, **tri** = 3, **tetra** = 4 (carbon dioxide = CO₂, carbon tetrachloride = CCl₄).

callouts.p: HCl, H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ appear in neutralisation, salt preparation and titration questions on both papers.

core.h: What an ion is and why it forms
core.p: An **ion** is an atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge because it has lost or gained electrons. Atoms lose or gain electrons to achieve a **full outer shell**, the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive; gaining electrons gives more electrons than protons, so the ion is negative.
bullets: **Metals** lose electrons and form **positive ions (cations)**.
**Non-metals** gain electrons and form **negative ions (anions)**.
The number of protons never changes when an ion forms: only electrons move.
Na (2.8.1) loses 1 electron → Na⁺ (2.8), same arrangement as neon.
Cl (2.8.7) gains 1 electron → Cl⁻ (2.8.8), same arrangement as argon.
The size of the charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained.

callouts.p: An ion is an atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost one or more electrons, so it has an overall charge.

core.h: Predicting ion charges from the periodic table
core.p: For main group elements the group number tells you the number of outer electrons, so it predicts the charge. Groups 1 to 3 lose their outer electrons (charge = group number, positive). Groups 5 to 7 gain enough electrons to reach 8 (charge = 8 minus group number, negative). Group 4 and group 0 do not usually form simple ions at GCSE.
bullets: Group 1: Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺.
Group 2: Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺.
Group 3: Al³⁺.
Group 5: N³⁻ (nitride).
Group 6: O²⁻ (oxide), S²⁻ (sulfide).
Group 7: F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ (fluoride, chloride, bromide, iodide).
Hydrogen forms H⁺ (in acids); this is just a proton.

callouts.p: Write the number before the sign as a superscript: Mg²⁺ not Mg⁺², and Cl⁻ not Cl⁻¹.

core.h: Transition metal ions and Roman numerals
core.p: Transition metals can form ions with **different charges**, so the group number cannot predict them. The name tells you the charge using a **Roman numeral** in brackets. Some other metals have a fixed charge you just need to learn.
bullets: Iron(II) = Fe²⁺, iron(III) = Fe³⁺.
Copper(II) = Cu²⁺ (copper(I) = Cu⁺ is less common).
Zinc always Zn²⁺, silver always Ag⁺, lead(II) Pb²⁺.
Example: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃, but iron(II) oxide is FeO.
The Roman numeral gives the charge on the metal ion, not the number of metal atoms in the formula.

callouts.p: Copper(II) chloride is CuCl₂, not Cu₂Cl. The (II) means each copper ion is 2+.

core.h: Compound (polyatomic) ions
core.p: A **compound ion** is a group of atoms covalently bonded together that carries an overall charge. It stays together as one unit in reactions and in formulae. You must recall these formulae and charges, because they cannot be worked out from the periodic table.
bullets: **Ammonium NH₄⁺** is the only common positive compound ion.
Hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻.
Sulfate SO₄²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻.
Hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻ is sometimes met (e.g. sodium hydrogencarbonate NaHCO₃).
Name endings: **-ide** usually means just the element (chloride Cl⁻, oxide O²⁻); **-ate** means the element is combined with oxygen (sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻).
Hydroxide is the exception: it ends in -ide but contains O and H.

callouts.p: Sulfide is S²⁻ (no oxygen). Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Mixing them up is one of the most common lost marks.

core.h: Working out the formula of an ionic compound
core.p: An ionic compound has **no overall charge**, so the total positive charge must exactly cancel the total negative charge. Choose the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that does this. This is why the formula of an ionic compound is a ratio (a **formula unit**), not a molecule.
bullets: Step 1: write the two ions with their charges, e.g. Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻.
Step 2: find how many of each make the charges cancel: one 2+ needs two 1− → MgCl₂.
Step 3: write the metal (positive ion) first, then the negative ion.
Shortcut 'swap and drop': the size of each charge becomes the other ion's subscript, then simplify (Mg²⁺ O²⁻ → Mg₂O₂ → MgO).
Always check: (number × charge) of positive ions + (number × charge) of negative ions = 0.
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl; Ca²⁺ + O²⁻ → CaO; Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃; K⁺ + O²⁻ → K₂O.

callouts.p: Swap and drop can give Ca₂O₂; always cancel to the simplest ratio, CaO.

core.h: Using brackets with compound ions
core.p: If you need more than one of a compound ion, put the whole ion in **brackets** and write the number outside. Without brackets the subscript would only multiply the last atom and change the ion into something else.
bullets: Calcium hydroxide: Ca²⁺ needs two OH⁻ → **Ca(OH)₂**. CaOH₂ is wrong.
Magnesium nitrate: Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ → **Mg(NO₃)₂**.
Ammonium sulfate: two NH₄⁺ for one SO₄²⁻ → **(NH₄)₂SO₄**.
Aluminium sulfate: two Al³⁺ (6+) and three SO₄²⁻ (6−) → **Al₂(SO₄)₃**.
No bracket is needed for one compound ion: NaOH, CaCO₃, NH₄Cl, KNO₃.
Counting atoms in Al₂(SO₄)₃: 2 Al, 3 S, 12 O = 17 atoms.

callouts.p: Do not write CaO₂H₂ or SO₈ to balance charges. The formula of the compound ion is fixed; only the number of ions changes.

core.h: Naming compounds from formulae (and back)
core.p: Names of ionic compounds give the metal (or ammonium) first, then the negative ion. Being fluent both ways lets you write formulae from word equations and identify products correctly.
bullets: KBr: potassium bromide. CuO: copper(II) oxide. FeCl₃: iron(III) chloride.
Na₂SO₄: sodium sulfate. CaCO₃: calcium carbonate. NH₄NO₃: ammonium nitrate.
Salts of hydrochloric acid are **chlorides**, of sulfuric acid **sulfates**, of nitric acid **nitrates**.
Two-element compounds end in -ide: magnesium oxide MgO, lithium nitride Li₃N, sodium sulfide Na₂S.
To deduce the charge of a transition metal from a formula, work backwards: in FeCl₃ three Cl⁻ give 3−, so iron is Fe³⁺, iron(III).

core.h: Molecules versus formula units (Higher-level reasoning)
core.p: For **simple covalent** substances the formula shows the actual number of atoms in one molecule (CH₄ really is one C bonded to four H). For **ionic** compounds there are no molecules: the formula shows the simplest **ratio** of ions in a giant ionic lattice. This explains why we never 'simplify' H₂O₂ to HO but always simplify ionic ratios like Mg₂O₂ to MgO.
bullets: Covalent molecular formula: actual atoms in a molecule (C₂H₆, H₂O₂, O₂).
Ionic formula: smallest whole-number ratio of ions (NaCl is 1:1 in a lattice of millions of ions).
This links to relative formula mass Mr, which is calculated from the formula, and to empirical formula work in Topic 1.
Metals and giant covalent substances (C, Si) are written as single symbols because they are huge lattices too.

callouts.p: Every mole calculation, balanced equation and Mr depends on a correct formula. One wrong subscript makes every later mark wrong too.

analogy.t: Ionic formulae as balancing a seesaw
analogy.p: Think of positive ions as weights on one side of a seesaw and negative ions as weights on the other; a 2+ ion is a 2 kg weight. A compound only forms when the seesaw is perfectly level, so a 2 kg Mg²⁺ needs two 1 kg Cl⁻ on the other side, giving MgCl₂. Compound ions are like sealed bags of weights: you can add more bags (brackets) but never open a bag and take bits out. Where it breaks down: a seesaw balances weights by position, but in real lattices the ions are arranged in 3D in every direction, and the formula is only a ratio, not a pair of ions sitting together.

terms.d: A substance made of only one type of atom, all with the same number of protons.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Symbols and numbers showing the elements in a substance and the number of atoms of each in one unit.
Two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds.
Describes a molecule made of two atoms, such as H₂, O₂ or Cl₂.
Exists as single, separate atoms, such as the noble gases He and Ar.
An atom or group of atoms with an overall charge because it has lost or gained electrons.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons (usually metals, and ammonium NH₄⁺).
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons (usually non-metals).
A group of covalently bonded atoms that carries an overall charge, such as SO₄²⁻ or NH₄⁺.
A compound made of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic attraction, with no overall charge.
The simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound, as shown by its formula.
The small number after a symbol or bracket giving how many of that atom or group are present.
The large number in front of a formula in an equation, showing how many units of that substance.
Shows the charge on a metal ion that can form more than one ion, e.g. iron(III) = Fe³⁺.
Shows a negative ion containing oxygen as well as another element, such as nitrate NO₃⁻.

mistakes.w: Oxygen gas is O.
mistakes.r: Oxygen is diatomic: O₂ (as are H₂, N₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂).

mistakes.w: Calcium hydroxide is CaOH₂.
mistakes.r: Ca(OH)₂: brackets show two whole hydroxide ions.

mistakes.w: Magnesium chloride is MgCl.
mistakes.r: MgCl₂, because Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions to cancel its charge.

mistakes.w: Sulfate is S²⁻ / sulfide is SO₄²⁻.
mistakes.r: Sulfide is S²⁻; sulfate is SO₄²⁻.

mistakes.w: Copper(II) oxide is Cu₂O.
mistakes.r: CuO: (II) means Cu²⁺, which balances one O²⁻.

mistakes.w: Magnesium ion is Mg⁺² or Mg2+ written on the line.
mistakes.r: Mg²⁺ with the number before the sign as a superscript.

mistakes.w: Aluminium oxide is AlO.
mistakes.r: Al₂O₃: two Al³⁺ (6+) balance three O²⁻ (6−).

mistakes.w: Ammonium ion is NH₃ or NH₄⁻.
mistakes.r: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ (ammonia, NH₃, is a neutral molecule).

mistakes.w: Writing cl, CL or co for chlorine/cobalt.
mistakes.r: First letter capital, second lower case: Cl, Co.

exam.q: Give the formula of a molecule of chlorine.
model: Cl₂
exam.tip: All halogens are diatomic as elements.

exam.q: Give the formula of the ion formed by a calcium atom.
model: Ca²⁺ (charge and sign both needed)
exam.tip: Calcium is in group 2, so it loses 2 electrons.

exam.q: Give the formula of the sulfate ion.
model: SO₄²⁻
exam.tip: Learn the compound ions; they cannot be worked out.

exam.q: Potassium reacts with oxygen to form potassium oxide. Write the formula of potassium oxide.
model: K₂O
exam.tip: K⁺ and O²⁻: two K⁺ are needed to balance one O²⁻.

exam.q: Write the formulae of (a) aluminium chloride and (b) iron(III) hydroxide.
model: (a) AlCl₃
(b) Fe(OH)₃ (brackets required)
exam.tip: Fe(III) is 3+, so it needs three OH⁻ in a bracket.

exam.q: A student writes the formula of magnesium nitrate as MgNO₃₂. Explain the error and give the correct formula.
model: Nitrate ion must be in brackets so the 2 multiplies the whole NO₃⁻ ion
Mg(NO₃)₂
exam.tip: Always bracket a compound ion when there is more than one.

exam.q: State the number of atoms of each element in one formula unit of (NH₄)₂SO₄.
exam.tip: Multiply every atom inside the bracket by the number outside.

exam.q: Explain why the formula of sodium oxide is Na₂O but the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.
model: Sodium is in group 1 so forms Na⁺ by losing one electron
Magnesium is in group 2 so forms Mg²⁺ by losing two electrons
Oxygen gains two electrons to form O²⁻
Compound has no overall charge, so two Na⁺ balance one O²⁻ but one Mg²⁺ balances one O²⁻
exam.tip: Link group number → electrons lost/gained → charge → ratio.

exam.q: Lithium (group 1) reacts with nitrogen (group 5) to form lithium nitride. Use ideas about electrons to deduce the formula of lithium nitride.
model: Lithium loses 1 electron to form Li⁺
Nitrogen gains 3 electrons to form N³⁻ (to achieve full outer shell)
Three Li⁺ needed to balance the charge on one N³⁻
Li₃N
exam.tip: Group 5 needs 3 more electrons to reach 8.

exam.q: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Name each compound and explain how the names show the difference between them.
model: FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride
FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride
Roman numeral shows the charge on the iron ion (Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺)
Each Cl⁻ is 1−, so 2 Cl⁻ balance Fe²⁺ and 3 Cl⁻ balance Fe³⁺
exam.tip: Transition metals can form more than one ion, hence the numeral.

exam.q: Describe how the formulae of elements, simple covalent compounds and ionic compounds are written, explaining the reasons for the differences. Use examples.
model: Metals and giant covalent elements written as single symbol, e.g. Fe, C, because they are giant structures
Noble gases monatomic, e.g. He, because full outer shells mean they do not bond
Diatomic elements written with subscript 2, e.g. O₂, Cl₂, because atoms share electrons in pairs
Simple covalent compound formulae show actual atoms in one molecule, e.g. H₂O, CH₄
Ionic formulae show simplest ratio of ions in a lattice, e.g. NaCl, MgCl₂
Ratio chosen so total positive charge equals total negative charge; brackets for more than one compound ion, e.g. Ca(OH)₂
exam.tip: For 6 marks, give a reason and an example for each type of substance.

worked.q: Work out the formula of aluminium sulfate.
steps: Aluminium is in group 3, so forms Al³⁺.
Sulfate is a compound ion: SO₄²⁻.
Lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6.
Two Al³⁺ give 6+; three SO₄²⁻ give 6−; total charge 0.
Sulfate is a compound ion and we need three of them, so use a bracket.

worked.q: Work out the formula of ammonium carbonate and count the total number of atoms in one formula unit.
steps: Ammonium is NH₄⁺; carbonate is CO₃²⁻.
Two NH₄⁺ (2+) balance one CO₃²⁻ (2−).
More than one ammonium ion, so bracket it: (NH₄)₂CO₃.

worked.q: A compound of copper and oxygen has the formula Cu₂O. Deduce the charge on the copper ion and name the compound.
steps: Oxide ion is O²⁻, so total negative charge = 2−.
Two copper ions must give a total of 2+.
Each copper ion is therefore 1+, Cu⁺.
The Roman numeral shows the charge on the metal ion.
worked.ans: Cu⁺; the compound is copper(I) oxide

chem_edx.0.1.summary: Chemical equations are the language of chemistry: a word equation names the reactants and products, while a balanced symbol equation shows the formulae and the ratio in which particles react. Because atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, a balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) add the physical state of each substance, which you must be able to choose correctly in both papers.

core.h: What a chemical equation shows
core.p: A chemical equation summarises a reaction. **Reactants** (starting substances) are written on the left and **products** (new substances made) on the right, joined by an arrow that means 'react to form'. Plus signs separate different substances on the same side; they do not mean 'add numbers'.
bullets: Reactants → products.
The arrow points from reactants to products; a reversible reaction uses ⇌ (met in later topics).
An equation tells you which substances react, what forms, and (when balanced) the **ratio of particles**.
Catalysts are not reactants, so they are not written as reactants; they may be written over the arrow.
Heat can be shown over the arrow for reactions that need heating, e.g. thermal decomposition.

callouts.p: Reactants are the substances present at the start of a reaction; products are the new substances formed by the reaction.

core.h: Writing word equations
core.p: A **word equation** uses the names of the substances only. It is the first step towards a symbol equation and is often worth a mark on its own. You must use correct chemical names (for example 'magnesium chloride', not 'magnesium and chlorine').
bullets: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
Do not include numbers, formulae or state symbols in a word equation.
Water must be written as 'water', not 'H₂O', in a word equation.

callouts.p: Answers such as 'magnesium + O₂ → MgO' do not earn the word equation mark. Use words only, or a full symbol equation.

core.h: General word equations you should recognise
core.p: Most GCSE reactions follow a few patterns. Knowing these lets you predict products in unfamiliar questions. The salt's name comes from the metal (or ammonium) plus the acid: hydrochloric acid gives **chlorides**, sulfuric acid gives **sulfates**, nitric acid gives **nitrates**.
bullets: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen
metal oxide + acid → salt + water
metal hydroxide + acid → salt + water (neutralisation)
metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide
metal + oxygen → metal oxide (oxidation)
hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (complete combustion)
metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide (thermal decomposition)
more reactive metal + salt of less reactive metal → new salt + less reactive metal (displacement)

core.h: Conservation of mass: why equations must balance
core.p: In a chemical reaction atoms are **rearranged** into new substances; no atoms are created or destroyed. So the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. A **balanced equation** shows this: it has the same number of atoms of each element on each side.
bullets: Law of conservation of mass: mass of reactants = mass of products (in a closed system).
Bonds between atoms are broken and new bonds are made, but the atoms themselves stay the same.
If mass seems to decrease, a gaseous product has escaped (e.g. CO₂ from a carbonate reacting with acid in an open flask).
If mass seems to increase, a gas from the air has been added (e.g. oxygen when magnesium burns to MgO).
Balancing numbers therefore reflect real particles, not just a maths puzzle.

callouts.p: In a chemical reaction no atoms are lost or made, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.

core.h: The golden rule of balancing
core.p: You balance an equation by placing **coefficients** (big numbers) in front of formulae. You must **never change a subscript** (small number) inside a formula, because that would change the substance itself. H₂O and H₂O₂ are different chemicals: water and hydrogen peroxide.
bullets: Coefficient: multiplies the whole formula. 2H₂O = 4 H atoms + 2 O atoms.
Subscript: part of the formula. Changing it changes the substance.
A coefficient of 1 is not written.
Use the smallest whole-number coefficients in the final answer.
Get the formulae right first (Topic 0.1), then balance.

callouts.p: Balancing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂O₂ on the right is wrong. Put a 2 in front: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

core.h: Step-by-step method for balancing
core.p: A systematic method avoids going round in circles. Count each type of atom on both sides, then adjust one coefficient at a time, recounting after every change.
bullets: 1. Write the correct formulae of all reactants and products.
2. Count atoms of each element on each side (a tally table helps).
3. Balance elements that appear in only one substance on each side first; leave elements on their own (O₂, H₂, metals) until last.
4. Treat a compound ion that appears unchanged on both sides (e.g. SO₄, NO₃, CO₃) as one unit.
5. Recount everything after each change.
6. If you have an odd number of O atoms but O₂ on the other side, double everything else (the odd/even trick).
7. Check that coefficients are the lowest possible whole numbers.

callouts.p: Writing a quick count table under the equation catches mistakes and keeps you calm under exam pressure.

core.h: Balancing examples from the course
core.p: These balanced equations come up repeatedly in both papers. Practise until you can balance them in seconds.
bullets: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (thermal decomposition)
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (Haber process)
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (halogen displacement)

core.h: State symbols
core.p: **State symbols** are written in brackets after each formula to show its physical state under the reaction conditions. Edexcel expects four symbols, and a question that asks for state symbols usually gives a separate mark for them.
bullets: **(s)** solid, e.g. Mg(s), CaCO₃(s), a precipitate such as AgCl(s).
**(l)** liquid, e.g. H₂O(l), Br₂(l), molten substances such as molten NaCl(l) in electrolysis.
**(g)** gas, e.g. H₂(g), O₂(g), CO₂(g), Cl₂(g).
**(aq)** aqueous: dissolved in water, e.g. HCl(aq), NaOH(aq), CuSO₄(aq).
Example: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

head: Symbol
Meaning
Typical examples
rows: acids, alkalis, soluble salts in water

callouts.p: Aqueous (aq) means dissolved in water.

core.h: Choosing the right state symbol (the reasoning)
core.p: Decide the state from what you know about the substance at room temperature and whether it dissolves. Water made in a reaction is a liquid, not aqueous: water cannot be dissolved in itself. Acids and alkalis in the lab are solutions, so they are (aq).
bullets: Water as a product at room temperature: **H₂O(l)**; as steam in combustion at high temperature it can be H₂O(g).
Soluble salts formed in solution: (aq), e.g. NaCl(aq), ZnSO₄(aq).
Insoluble salts formed when two solutions mix are **precipitates**: (s), e.g. BaSO₄(s), AgCl(s).
Metals and metal oxides added to acids are usually (s).
Halogens: Cl₂(g), Br₂(l) as the element, but they are (aq) when given as chlorine water or bromine water.
Molten ionic compounds in electrolysis are (l), e.g. PbBr₂(l).

callouts.p: Pure water is a liquid: H₂O(l). Writing H₂O(aq) is a common lost mark.

core.h: What a balanced equation tells you (ratios)
core.p: The coefficients show the **ratio of particles**, and therefore the ratio of **moles**, that react and form. This is the basis of all reacting-mass calculations in Topic 1. The equation does not tell you the rate, the energy change or the masses directly.
bullets: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 2 molecules of H₂ react with 1 molecule of O₂ to give 2 molecules of H₂O.
In moles: 2 mol H₂ : 1 mol O₂ : 2 mol H₂O.
Mass is conserved: total Mr × coefficients on the left equals that on the right (4 + 32 = 36).
Higher tier link: you may be asked to deduce the balancing numbers from given reacting masses, by converting masses to moles and finding the simplest whole-number ratio.

callouts.p: The big numbers in a balanced equation give the ratio of moles reacting, which you use in calculations later in the course.

core.h: Translating a description into an equation
core.p: Exam questions often describe a reaction in words and ask for a balanced equation with state symbols. Work in a fixed order so nothing is missed.
bullets: 1. Identify reactants and products from the text (look for clues: 'fizzing' means a gas; 'white solid forms' means a precipitate (s)).
2. Write the word equation.
3. Convert each name to a correct formula.
4. Balance.
5. Add state symbols from the description.
Example: sodium burns in chlorine to form sodium chloride → 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s).

callouts.p: Words like 'solution', 'dissolved', 'bubbles', 'precipitate' and 'molten' are telling you the state symbols.

analogy.t: Equations as a recipe with LEGO bricks
analogy.p: Imagine building models from LEGO bricks: you take apart some models (reactants) and rebuild the same bricks into new models (products). You can never magic up extra bricks or throw any away, so the number of each colour of brick before and after must match; that is balancing. You can build more copies of a model (coefficients), but you cannot change the design of a model to make the count work (subscripts). Where it breaks down: LEGO bricks are just pushed together, whereas real atoms rearrange by breaking and making bonds with energy changes, and real atoms in ionic compounds are charged ions rather than neutral blocks.

terms.d: A substance present at the start of a reaction that is used up.
A new substance formed in a chemical reaction.
An equation that shows the names of reactants and products only.
An equation that uses chemical formulae to show reactants and products.
A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
A number placed in front of a formula to balance an equation; it multiplies the whole formula.
The small number within a formula showing how many atoms; it must not be changed when balancing.
No atoms are made or destroyed in a reaction, so total mass of products equals total mass of reactants.
A system where no substances can enter or leave, so the measured mass stays constant.
A symbol in brackets after a formula showing its state: (s), (l), (g) or (aq).
Dissolved in water.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed; given the state symbol (s).
A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
The breaking down of a substance into simpler substances by heating.
The ratio of the numbers of moles of substances in a reaction, given by the coefficients in the balanced equation.

mistakes.w: Balancing by changing subscripts, e.g. H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂.
mistakes.r: Change only coefficients: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

mistakes.w: Writing H₂O(aq) for water formed in a neutralisation.
mistakes.r: H₂O(l): water is a liquid, it cannot be 'dissolved in water'.

mistakes.w: Writing Cl or O for chlorine and oxygen gas.
mistakes.r: Cl₂(g) and O₂(g): these elements are diatomic.

mistakes.w: Word equation including formulae, e.g. 'zinc + HCl'.
mistakes.r: Words only: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Naming the salt from sulfuric acid as a 'sulfide' or 'sulphurate'.
mistakes.r: Sulfuric acid forms sulfates, e.g. zinc sulfate.

mistakes.w: Giving a precipitate the symbol (aq).
mistakes.r: A precipitate is an insoluble solid: (s), e.g. BaSO₄(s).

mistakes.w: Leaving coefficients that can be simplified, e.g. 4Mg + 2O₂ → 4MgO.
mistakes.r: Lowest whole numbers: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

mistakes.w: Saying mass is lost because atoms are destroyed when a gas is made.
mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; the gas escaped from the open container so it was not weighed.

mistakes.w: Counting 2H₂O as 2 H and 1 O.
mistakes.r: The coefficient multiplies everything: 4 H and 2 O.

exam.q: State what the symbol (aq) means.
model: Dissolved in water / aqueous solution
exam.tip: 'Aqueous' alone is fine, but 'liquid' is wrong.

exam.q: Write the word equation for the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid.
model: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
exam.tip: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.

exam.q: Balance the equation: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
model: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
exam.tip: Odd O on the right: double Al₂O₃ first, then fix the others.

exam.q: Balance the equation: Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂
model: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
exam.tip: Each CO takes one O from the iron oxide; three O to remove means 3CO.

exam.q: Complete the balanced equation with state symbols for the reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
model: 2 in front of HCl (balancing)
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) (all state symbols correct)
exam.tip: Balancing and state symbols are usually separate marks.

exam.q: When copper carbonate is heated in an open tube, the mass of solid decreases. Explain why, using ideas about conservation of mass.
model: Carbon dioxide gas is produced (CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂)
The gas escapes into the air so is not weighed; total mass of products still equals mass of reactants
exam.tip: Never say atoms or mass are 'lost' or 'destroyed'.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium hydroxide solution with sulfuric acid.
model: Correct formulae: NaOH, H₂SO₄, Na₂SO₄, H₂O
Balanced: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
State symbols: (aq) + (aq) → (aq) + (l)
exam.tip: Sodium sulfate needs two Na⁺ for one SO₄²⁻.

exam.q: Silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution. A white precipitate of silver chloride forms. Write the balanced equation with state symbols.
model: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃
AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
exam.tip: 'Precipitate' tells you (s).

exam.q: Ethane, C₂H₆, burns completely in oxygen. Write the balanced equation and explain how you balanced it.
model: C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O correct products
Balance C: 2CO₂; balance H: 3H₂O
Oxygen on right = 7, odd, so double everything
2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
exam.tip: Leave O₂ until last because it is an element on its own.

exam.q: A student writes the equation Na + H₂O → NaOH + H. Identify two errors and write the correct balanced equation with state symbols.
model: Hydrogen should be H₂ (diatomic)
Equation is not balanced / missing coefficients
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
exam.tip: Check formulae first, then balancing, then states.

exam.q: Explain why a chemical equation must be balanced and why only the numbers in front of formulae may be changed when balancing. Use the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen to illustrate your answer.
model: In a reaction atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed
So mass is conserved: same number of each atom on both sides
Unbalanced H₂ + O₂ → H₂O has 2 O on left but 1 on right
Changing a subscript (e.g. H₂O₂) changes the substance, so it is not allowed
Coefficients change the number of molecules: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Coefficients show the ratio of molecules/moles reacting (2:1:2), giving 4 H and 2 O on each side
exam.tip: Link conservation of atoms → balancing → meaning of coefficients.

worked.q: Write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈.
steps: Word equation: propane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Formulae: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
Balance C: 3 C on left, so 3CO₂.
Balance H: 8 H on left, so 4H₂O.
Count O on right: (3 × 2) + (4 × 1) = 10, so 5O₂.
States: propane and oxygen are gases; water at room temperature is liquid.
Treat SO₄ and OH as units.
Al: 2 on left, so 2Al(OH)₃.
SO₄: 3 on left, so 3Na₂SO₄.
Na: 3 × 2 = 6 on right, so 6NaOH.
OH: 6 on left, 2 × 3 = 6 on right. Balanced.

worked.q: Show that mass is conserved in 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
steps: Mr of MgO = 24 + 16 = 40.
Mass of products = 2 × 40 = 80.
Reactants = products, so mass is conserved.
worked.ans: 80 g of reactants gives 80 g of product, so mass is conserved

chem_edx.0.2.summary: When ionic compounds dissolve in water their ions separate and move freely, and in many reactions only some of those ions actually change. A balanced ionic equation shows just the particles that react and the products they form, leaving out the spectator ions that are present but unchanged. Ionic equations must balance for both atoms and charge, and they reveal why apparently different reactions, such as every acid-alkali neutralisation, are really the same reaction: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

core.h: Why we need ionic equations
core.p: A full symbol equation lists whole compounds, but in solution ionic compounds are split into separate ions. Many of these ions take no part in the reaction. An **ionic equation** strips the reaction down to the particles that really change, so it shows what is chemically happening.
bullets: Ionic compounds that are **dissolved (aq)** exist as separate, freely moving ions.
In a reaction, some ions combine to form a new substance (a solid, a gas, water or a covalent molecule) or change by gaining or losing electrons.
Other ions stay exactly the same, dissolved in solution, before and after: these are **spectator ions**.
The ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions.
It shows that, for example, HCl + NaOH and HNO₃ + KOH are the same reaction at particle level.

callouts.p: An equation that shows only the ions and other particles that take part in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
An ion that is present in the reaction mixture but does not take part in the reaction; it is unchanged and appears on both sides of the full ionic equation.

core.h: Which substances split into ions (and which do not)
core.p: The key decision is what to write as separate ions. Only **ionic compounds in aqueous solution** (and acids in solution) are split. Anything that is a solid, a liquid, a gas or a covalent molecule is written as its full formula, because its particles are not free separate ions in the solution.
bullets: Split: soluble salts (aq), e.g. CuSO₄(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq).
Split: alkalis (aq), e.g. NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Split: acids (aq), e.g. HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq).
Do NOT split: solids and precipitates, e.g. AgCl(s), CaCO₃(s), Zn(s).
Do NOT split: water H₂O(l) and other covalent molecules.
Do NOT split: gases such as CO₂(g), H₂(g), Cl₂(g), and elements like Br₂(aq) (a covalent molecule dissolved).

callouts.p: One formula unit of CaCl₂(aq) gives Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, and Na₂SO₄(aq) gives 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻. The subscript becomes a coefficient for that ion.

core.h: Method: from full equation to ionic equation
core.p: Follow the same four steps every time. Starting from a correct balanced equation with state symbols is essential, because the state symbols tell you what can be split.
bullets: Step 1: write the **balanced symbol equation with state symbols**.
Step 2: rewrite every (aq) ionic compound and acid as its separate ions (keep the correct numbers).
Step 3: **cancel spectator ions**: any ion that appears identically on both sides.
Step 4: write what is left, then simplify coefficients if they share a common factor.
Step 5: check that **atoms balance** and that the **total charge is the same** on both sides.

callouts.p: Add up the charges on each side. If they are not equal, the ionic equation is wrong even if the atoms balance.

core.h: Neutralisation: acid + alkali
core.p: Every reaction between an acid and an alkali has the same ionic equation. Acids in solution provide **hydrogen ions H⁺(aq)** and alkalis provide **hydroxide ions OH⁻(aq)**. These combine to make water; the metal ion and the acid's negative ion are spectators that stay in solution as the salt.
bullets: Full: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l).
Ions: H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l).
Cancel Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (spectators).
Ionic: **H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)**.
With sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O gives 2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O, which simplifies to H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
This explains why neutralising the same number of moles of H⁺ by any alkali gives similar energy changes.

callouts.p: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) is the ionic equation for all acid + alkali neutralisations.

core.h: Precipitation reactions
core.p: When two solutions are mixed and an **insoluble** product forms, it appears as a solid **precipitate**. The ionic equation shows just the two ions that come together to form the solid. All other ions remain dissolved and are spectators.
bullets: Silver nitrate + sodium chloride: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq).
Ionic: **Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)** (white precipitate); Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.
Bromide: Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) (cream); iodide: Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s) (yellow).
Sulfate test: **Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)** (white precipitate).
Insoluble salt preparation, e.g. Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s).
Metal hydroxides: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) (blue); Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s) (green); Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) (brown).

core.h: Acids reacting with metals and carbonates
core.p: Acids react because of their **H⁺ ions**, so the acid's negative ion (Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻) is usually a spectator. Pay attention to whether the metal or carbonate is a solid, because solids are not split.
bullets: Metal + acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) gives **Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)**.
Zinc: Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g) (whichever acid is used).
Solid carbonate: CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Carbonate in solution: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) gives **2H⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)**.
Charge check for Mg: left 2+ (2 × H⁺), right 2+ (Mg²⁺). Balanced.

callouts.p: CaCO₃ is a solid, so writing Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ on the left is wrong; it stays as CaCO₃(s).

core.h: Metal displacement reactions
core.p: A more reactive metal **displaces** a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. The negative ion of the salt is a spectator, so the ionic equation shows electrons being transferred from one metal to the other: the more reactive metal atom becomes an ion, and the less reactive metal ion becomes an atom.
bullets: Full: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s).
Ionic: **Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)**; SO₄²⁻ is the spectator.
Mg(s) + Fe²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Fe(s).
Uneven charges need balancing: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).
Zinc loses electrons (oxidised); copper ions gain electrons (reduced): this is a **redox** reaction.

callouts.p: In Cu + Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Ag, the atoms balance but the charge does not (1+ vs 2+). Put 2 in front of Ag⁺ and Ag.

core.h: Halogen displacement reactions
core.p: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions. The metal ion (e.g. K⁺ or Na⁺) is a spectator. Halogens themselves are covalent diatomic molecules, so they are written as X₂ and never split.
bullets: Full: Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq).
Ionic: **Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)**; K⁺ is the spectator.
Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq).
Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq).
Charge: left 2− (two Br⁻), right 2− (two Cl⁻). Balanced.
The more reactive halogen gains electrons (is reduced) and the halide ion loses electrons (is oxidised).

core.h: Balancing ionic equations: atoms and charge
core.p: An ionic equation must obey two conservation laws at once. **Atoms** are conserved, just like any equation, and **charge** is conserved, because electrons cannot appear from nowhere. The total charge does not have to be zero, but it must be equal on both sides.
bullets: Count each type of atom on both sides.
Add the charges on each side: e.g. 2H⁺ is 2+, CO₃²⁻ is 2−, so the left of 2H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ totals 0.
Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s): left 3+ + 3− = 0, right 0.
If charges do not match, adjust coefficients of the ions, never their charges.
Simplify to the lowest whole-number ratio at the end (2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O becomes H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O).
Include state symbols when asked; they are usually needed in the final ionic equation.

callouts.p: A correct ionic equation balances atoms AND balances total charge.

core.h: Links to half equations (Higher tier)
core.p: Redox ionic equations can be broken into two **half equations** that show electrons (e⁻) explicitly. These are used in electrolysis and in explaining oxidation and reduction. Adding the two half equations, with equal numbers of electrons, gives back the ionic equation.
bullets: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation: loss of electrons).
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction: gain of electrons).
Add them: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu (electrons cancel).
Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
Half equations themselves belong to the electrolysis and redox topics; here you only need to see how they fit the ionic equation.

core.h: Identifying spectator ions in exam questions
core.p: Examiners often give a full equation and ask you to name the spectator ions or to explain why they are left out. Use the full ionic form and look for ions that are identical, with the same state, on both sides.
bullets: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): spectator = SO₄²⁻.
BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq): spectators = Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
HNO₃(aq) + KOH(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l): spectators = K⁺ and NO₃⁻.
Explanation phrase: 'they are present in solution before and after the reaction and do not change'.
An ion that becomes part of a solid, a gas or water is NOT a spectator.

callouts.p: Say spectator ions 'do not take part in the reaction' or 'are unchanged'. Saying they 'are not there' is wrong: they are present but unchanged.

analogy.p: Picture a hall full of pupils (ions) mixing freely. When the music starts, a few pupils pair up and leave the floor to dance together: they are the reacting ions forming a product such as AgCl(s) or H₂O. Everyone else is still standing around the edge exactly as before: the spectators. The ionic equation is the photo of just the couples who paired up, because they are the only change that happened. Where it breaks down: spectator ions are not just bystanders that can be removed, because their charges keep the solution neutral overall, and some ionic reactions involve electrons transferring rather than ions simply pairing up.

terms.d: An atom or group of atoms with an overall charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
An equation showing only the particles that react and form, with spectator ions removed.
An ion present in the reaction mixture that does not take part in the reaction and is unchanged.
A solution in which water is the solvent; dissolved ionic compounds exist as separate free ions.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.
A reaction in which two solutions react to form an insoluble solid.
The reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water; ionically H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
The ion released by acids in aqueous solution; responsible for acidic properties.
The ion released by alkalis in aqueous solution.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
The total charge on the reactant side of an ionic equation equals the total charge on the product side.
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen).
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen).
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time.
An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons.

mistakes.w: Splitting a precipitate: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → Ag⁺ + Cl⁻.
mistakes.r: The product is a solid and stays together: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

mistakes.w: Splitting water into H⁺ + OH⁻ on the product side.
mistakes.r: Water is covalent and is written H₂O(l).

mistakes.w: Writing CaCO₃ as Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ when solid calcium carbonate reacts with acid.
mistakes.r: Solids are not split: CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).

mistakes.w: Cu + Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Ag (atoms balance so it is correct).
mistakes.r: Charge must balance too: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag.

mistakes.w: Splitting chlorine: Cl⁺ + Cl⁻ or 2Cl⁻ on the reactant side for Cl₂.
mistakes.r: Halogens are covalent molecules: write Cl₂(aq).

mistakes.w: Spectator ions are 'ions that are not there'.
mistakes.r: They are present in solution but do not take part / remain unchanged.

mistakes.w: Leaving 2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O unsimplified.
mistakes.r: Simplify to H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

mistakes.w: Writing sodium sulfate as Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻ when split.
mistakes.r: Na₂SO₄(aq) gives 2Na⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq).

mistakes.w: Including the spectator ion, e.g. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, as the 'ionic equation'.
mistakes.r: Remove SO₄²⁻: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).

exam.q: What is meant by a spectator ion?
model: An ion that is present but does not take part in the reaction / is unchanged
exam.tip: 'Present but unchanged' is the key idea.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali. Include state symbols.
model: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
State symbols (aq) + (aq) → (l)
exam.tip: One mark often depends on state symbols.

exam.q: Silver nitrate solution is added to potassium iodide solution and a yellow precipitate forms. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols.
model: Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI
Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s)
exam.tip: The precipitate is always (s).

exam.q: Identify the spectator ions in: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
model: Na⁺
Cl⁻
exam.tip: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form the solid, so they are not spectators.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction between zinc and copper(II) sulfate solution.
model: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Correct state symbols: Zn(s), Cu²⁺(aq), Zn²⁺(aq), Cu(s)
exam.tip: Sulfate is the spectator.

exam.q: Complete and balance the ionic equation: Cl₂(aq) + ...Br⁻(aq) → ...Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)
model: Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)
exam.tip: Two atoms in each halogen molecule means two halide ions.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium ribbon with dilute sulfuric acid.
model: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
Correct balancing with 2H⁺ (charge balanced)
exam.tip: Sulfate is a spectator whichever acid is used.

exam.q: A student writes the ionic equation Fe³⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s). Explain what is wrong and correct it.
model: Equation is not balanced: 3 OH groups on right but only 1 on left
Charge not balanced (2+ on left, 0 on right)
Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
exam.tip: Check both atoms and charge.

exam.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium carbonate solution. Derive the ionic equation for this reaction, showing your working.
model: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ions: 2Na⁺ + CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → 2Na⁺ + 2Cl⁻ + H₂O + CO₂
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cancelled as spectators
2H⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
exam.tip: Show the full ionic line: method marks are available.

exam.q: Explain why the reactions of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide and of nitric acid with potassium hydroxide have the same ionic equation.
model: Both acids release H⁺ ions in solution; both alkalis release OH⁻ ions
The reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ forming H₂O
The other ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻ / K⁺, NO₃⁻) are spectator ions
Spectators are unchanged so are left out, leaving H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) in both cases
exam.tip: Name the spectators for each reaction.

exam.q: Describe how to write a balanced ionic equation for a reaction, using the reaction between solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide (forming insoluble lead(II) iodide) as an example.
model: Write balanced full equation: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq)
Split dissolved ionic compounds into ions: Pb²⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ + 2K⁺ + 2I⁻
Do not split the solid precipitate PbI₂(s)
Identify K⁺ and NO₃⁻ as spectator ions and cancel them
Write ionic equation: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s)
Check atoms and charges balance (left 2+ and 2− = 0; right 0)
exam.tip: Structure your answer as numbered steps and finish with the check.

worked.q: Derive the ionic equation for the reaction of sulfuric acid with potassium hydroxide solution.
steps: Full: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
Split: 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2K⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2K⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
Cancel spectators K⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
Left: 2H⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l).
Divide by 2 to simplify.
Check: charge left 0, right 0; atoms 2 H and 1 O each side.

worked.q: Copper metal is placed in silver nitrate solution. Silver crystals and a blue solution of copper(II) nitrate form. Write the balanced ionic equation.
steps: Full: Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s).
Split: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) + 2NO₃⁻(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2NO₃⁻(aq) + 2Ag(s).
Cancel NO₃⁻ (spectator).
Check atoms: 1 Cu, 2 Ag each side.
Check charge: left 2 × (1+) = 2+, right 2+.

worked.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution and a brown precipitate forms. Write the ionic equation.
steps: Full: FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq).
Split: Fe³⁺ + 3Cl⁻ + 3Na⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3Na⁺ + 3Cl⁻.
Cancel Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

chem_edx.0.3.summary: Hazard symbols are standard red-bordered diamond pictograms that warn you what a chemical can do to you or the environment: explosive, flammable, oxidising, corrosive, toxic, harmful/irritant, serious health hazard and environmental hazard. In every practical you must be able to identify the **hazard** (the thing that could cause harm), judge the **risk** (how likely harm is and how bad it would be) and suggest a **precaution** that reduces that risk. Top answers always link a specific hazard to a specific precaution and explain why the precaution works.

core.h: Why hazard symbols exist
core.p: Chemicals are labelled with internationally agreed pictograms so that anyone, in any country, can see at a glance what kind of danger a substance poses without needing to read a language. Each symbol is a black picture inside a white diamond with a red border.
bullets: The symbols come from the **Globally Harmonised System (GHS)**, so the same symbol means the same thing everywhere.
A symbol tells you the **type** of hazard, not how dangerous a given amount is: concentration and quantity also matter.
One substance can carry **more than one** symbol, e.g. concentrated nitric acid is both corrosive and oxidising.
You must be able to **recall** what each symbol means and **suggest precautions** linked to it.
Older textbooks show orange square symbols; exam papers now use the red diamond style, but the meanings are the same.

callouts.p: Something (a substance, object or activity) that has the potential to cause harm.
The chance that someone will be harmed by a hazard, combined with how serious the harm would be.

core.h: The hazard symbols and what they mean
core.p: Learn each symbol, its meaning and a typical example from school chemistry. The examples help you write precautions that make sense in context.
bullets: **Explosive**: may explode if heated, struck or ignited.
**Flammable**: catches fire easily; keep away from naked flames and sparks.
**Oxidising**: provides oxygen (or accepts electrons) so makes other materials burn more fiercely; keep away from flammable substances.
**Corrosive**: destroys living tissue such as skin and eyes, and can attack materials such as metals.
**Toxic**: can cause death or serious illness if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through the skin, even in small amounts.
**Harmful / irritant** (exclamation mark): may cause irritation, reddening or blistering of skin, or illness, but is less dangerous than toxic.
**Serious health hazard**: can cause long-term harm such as cancer, damage to organs or breathing problems.
**Environmental hazard**: harmful to aquatic life and the environment; must not be poured down the sink.

core.h: More symbols: oxidising, harmful, health and environment
core.p: These four are just as likely to appear. Students often confuse oxidising with flammable and harmful with toxic, so learn the differences carefully.
bullets: The **oxidising** symbol shows a flame **above a circle** (the circle represents oxygen); the flammable symbol is a flame on a line.
The **exclamation mark** means harmful or irritant: less severe than the skull and crossbones.
The **serious health hazard** symbol shows a person with a star-shaped burst on the chest.
The **environmental hazard** symbol shows a dead tree and a dead fish.
Oxidisers are not flammable themselves, but they make fires much more intense because they supply oxygen.

callouts.p: An oxidising substance does not itself burn. It supplies oxygen so that OTHER substances burn more fiercely. Do not write 'catches fire easily' for oxidising.

core.h: Hazard, risk and precaution: the key distinction
core.p: Mark schemes separate three ideas. The **hazard** is what could cause harm. The **risk** is how likely and how serious the harm is in this particular experiment. The **precaution** (control measure) is what you do to reduce the risk. You cannot remove a hazard just by being careful, but you can reduce the risk.
bullets: Hazard: concentrated sulfuric acid is **corrosive**.
Risk: it could splash into your eyes or onto your skin when you pour it, causing burns.
Precaution: wear **safety goggles** and gloves, pour carefully from a small bottle, or use a **more dilute** acid.
A good precaution reduces either the **chance** of harm (e.g. using a fume cupboard so gas is not breathed in) or the **severity** of harm (e.g. using a lower concentration).
Replacing a hazardous chemical with a less hazardous one is often the best precaution of all.

callouts.p: For full marks always give: the hazard, what could happen (the risk), and a precaution that is specific and explains how it reduces the risk.

core.h: Writing a risk assessment
core.p: A **risk assessment** is carried out before a practical. It lists each hazard, the harm it could cause, and the precautions that reduce the risk to an acceptable level. It also includes what to do if something goes wrong.
bullets: Step 1: **identify the hazards** for every chemical and piece of apparatus (hot objects, glass, electricity, gases).
Step 2: decide **who could be harmed and how** (splashes, inhaling fumes, burns, cuts).
Step 3: **evaluate the risk**: how likely, how serious, and does quantity or concentration matter?
Step 4: choose **precautions** that reduce the risk.
Step 5: plan **emergency action**, e.g. wash skin with plenty of cold water, use an eye wash, tell the teacher.
Risk depends on **concentration**, **volume/mass**, **temperature** and whether gases are produced.

core.h: General laboratory safety rules
core.p: Some precautions apply to almost every chemistry practical. They are worth marks only when they are relevant, so link them to a hazard rather than listing them all.
bullets: Wear **safety goggles** (eye protection) whenever chemicals are used or heated: eyes are damaged very easily and permanently.
Tie back long hair and tuck in ties or loose clothing near a Bunsen burner.
Stand up during practicals so you can move away quickly if something spills or catches fire.
Never eat or drink in the lab; wash hands after handling chemicals.
Keep bags and stools out of the way to avoid tripping.
Report all breakages and spills; clear up broken glass with a dustpan, not your hands.
Use the **smallest amounts** and **lowest concentrations** that still give a result.
Dispose of chemicals as instructed; heavy metal salts and environmental hazards go into labelled waste containers.

callouts.p: 'Be careful' or 'wear safety equipment' do not gain marks. Name the equipment (safety goggles, gloves, fume cupboard) and say what it protects against.

core.h: Heating safely: Bunsen burners and water baths
core.p: Many risks in practicals come from heating. The precaution depends on what is being heated and whether anything flammable is nearby.
bullets: Light a Bunsen with the **air hole closed** to give a visible yellow **safety flame**; open the air hole for a hot blue flame when heating.
Put the Bunsen back on the safety flame when not in use so it is easy to see.
Heat test tubes **at an angle**, pointing away from yourself and others, and shake gently so the liquid does not spit out suddenly.
Use **tongs** or a holder for hot objects; hot glass looks the same as cold glass.
**Flammable liquids** such as ethanol must be heated with a **water bath** or electric heater, never directly over a flame.
When evaporating a salt solution, stop heating before it is dry so the crystals do not **spit** hot solid out of the basin.
Add **anti-bumping granules** when boiling liquids (e.g. distillation) so they boil smoothly rather than violently.

callouts.p: A water bath cannot get hotter than 100 C and has no naked flame, so the vapour of a flammable solvent cannot be ignited.

core.h: Toxic and harmful gases: fume cupboards and ventilation
core.p: Gases spread through the room and are breathed in, so the main precaution is to stop them reaching people. A **fume cupboard** draws gas away from the user and out of the building.
bullets: **Chlorine** (produced in electrolysis of sodium chloride solution or tested for with damp litmus) is **toxic**: use small amounts, work in a fume cupboard or a well-ventilated room.
**Sulfur dioxide** is produced when sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid in the rates practical; it irritates lungs, so ventilate the room and take extra care with **asthmatics**.
**Ammonia** solution gives off an irritating gas; keep the bottle stoppered and use in a ventilated area.
**Hydrogen** is flammable and forms an explosive mixture with air: keep flames away and only collect small volumes.
Never smell a gas directly; waft it gently towards your nose only if the teacher says it is safe.

callouts.p: Use a fume cupboard whenever a toxic or harmful gas is produced in more than tiny amounts. It removes the gas so it cannot be inhaled.

core.h: Corrosive and irritant liquids: acids and alkalis
core.p: Acids and alkalis appear in many practicals, such as titration, making salts and electrolysis. Their hazard depends strongly on concentration.
bullets: **Concentrated** acids and alkalis are **corrosive**; **dilute** ones are usually **irritant**.
**Alkalis** such as sodium hydroxide are especially dangerous to eyes because they damage tissue quickly: always wear goggles.
Fill burettes **below eye level** (remove from the stand or use a funnel carefully) so acid or alkali cannot splash into your eyes.
Use a **pipette filler**, never your mouth, when using a pipette.
If acid or alkali touches skin, **wash with plenty of cold running water**.
Choose the **lowest concentration** that still works to reduce the severity of any splash.

core.h: Applying safety to Edexcel core practicals
core.p: Edexcel expects you to evaluate the risks in its core practicals. Know the main hazard and best precaution for each.
bullets: Use **small amounts**, a **safety screen** and goggles whenever reactive metals are demonstrated.
Always link each precaution to a reason so the examiner sees you understand the risk.

core.h: Reactive metals and explosive mixtures
core.p: Some reactions are dangerous because they release energy very quickly. The precaution is to limit the amount and put a barrier between the reaction and people.
bullets: Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) react vigorously with water to make **flammable hydrogen** and a corrosive alkali.
Use only a **small piece** of metal, a large volume of water, a **safety screen** and goggles.
Store alkali metals **under oil** so they cannot react with air or water vapour.
Hydrogen and oxygen mixtures **explode** when ignited (the squeaky pop test uses only a test tube full).
Never heat a sealed container: pressure builds up and it can burst.

core.h: Evaluating risk: quantity, concentration and alternatives
core.p: Grade 9 answers do not just list precautions; they **evaluate** whether the risk is acceptable and how to lower it further. The same chemical can be low risk in one experiment and high risk in another.
bullets: Risk rises with **concentration**: 0.1 mol dm-3 hydrochloric acid is far less dangerous than 10 mol dm-3.
Risk rises with **quantity**: a few drops of ethanol on a watch glass is lower risk than a beaker of it.
Risk rises with **temperature**: hot acid causes worse burns and gives off more fumes.
Risk rises when **gas** is made, because it can be inhaled by everyone in the room.

The most effective precautions are **elimination or substitution** (use a safer chemical), then **engineering controls** (fume cupboard, screen, water bath), then **personal protective equipment** (goggles, gloves, lab coat).
Goggles do not reduce the chance of a splash; they reduce the harm if one happens.

callouts.p: If an experiment still works with a more dilute solution, smaller quantities or a less hazardous substance, that is the best way to reduce risk.

analogy.p: A busy road is the **hazard**: it can always hurt you. How likely you are to be hurt depends on how you cross it, which is the **risk**. Using a pedestrian crossing, looking both ways and wearing bright clothing are **precautions** that lower the risk without removing the road. The hazard symbol is like a road sign telling you what kind of danger to expect. The analogy breaks down because chemical hazards can also harm people who are not involved (toxic gases spread through a room), and because you can often swap a chemical for a safer one, whereas you cannot swap the road.

terms.d: Something that has the potential to cause harm.
The likelihood that a hazard will cause harm, together with how serious that harm would be.
An action taken to reduce the risk from a hazard (also called a control measure).
A written check, done before a practical, that identifies hazards, evaluates the risks and lists precautions and emergency actions.
A standard pictogram (black image in a red-bordered diamond) showing the type of danger a substance poses.
Destroys living tissue such as skin and eyes, and can attack materials.
Can cause death or serious harm if swallowed, inhaled or absorbed through the skin, even in small amounts.
May cause irritation, inflammation or illness, but is less dangerous than toxic.
Catches fire easily.
Provides oxygen that allows other substances to burn more fiercely.
May explode, releasing energy and gas very rapidly, if heated, ignited or struck.
Harmful to the environment, especially aquatic life; must not be poured down the sink.
May cause long-term harm such as cancer, organ damage or breathing problems.
An enclosed workspace with a fan that removes toxic or harmful gases away from the user.
The yellow, luminous Bunsen flame produced with the air hole closed; easy to see.
Small pieces added to a liquid before boiling so that it boils smoothly instead of violently.

mistakes.w: Oxidising means it catches fire easily.
mistakes.r: Oxidising means it provides oxygen so other substances burn more fiercely; flammable means it catches fire easily.

mistakes.w: Be careful with the acid.
mistakes.r: A named precaution with a reason, e.g. wear safety goggles to protect eyes from corrosive acid splashes.

mistakes.w: Wear safety equipment.
mistakes.r: Name the specific equipment: safety goggles, gloves, a safety screen or a fume cupboard.

mistakes.w: Hazard and risk mean the same thing.
mistakes.r: Hazard is what could cause harm; risk is the chance of harm and how serious it would be.

mistakes.w: Heat the ethanol with a Bunsen burner.
mistakes.r: Heat flammable liquids using a water bath or electric heater, with no naked flames nearby.

mistakes.w: The exclamation mark means toxic.
mistakes.r: The exclamation mark means harmful or irritant; toxic is the skull and crossbones.

mistakes.w: Wear goggles so the acid does not splash.
mistakes.r: Goggles do not stop splashes; they protect the eyes if a splash occurs.

mistakes.w: Do the experiment in a fume cupboard so it is safer (for a reaction that makes no gas).
mistakes.r: A fume cupboard is the right precaution only when a toxic or harmful gas or vapour is produced.

mistakes.w: Pour leftover copper sulfate down the sink.
mistakes.r: Copper sulfate is an environmental hazard, so it goes into a labelled waste container.

exam.q: State the meaning of the hazard symbol showing a skull and crossbones.
model: Toxic (can cause death or serious harm in small amounts).
exam.tip: Use the exact word 'toxic', not 'dangerous' or 'poisonous gas'.

exam.q: Concentrated sulfuric acid carries the corrosive symbol. State what corrosive means.
model: Destroys / attacks living tissue such as skin and eyes.
exam.tip: Mention living tissue (skin or eyes); 'burns things' is too vague.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk.
model: A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm.
A risk is the chance of harm happening (and how serious it would be).
exam.tip: Two separate definitions are needed for two marks.

exam.q: A student heats ethanol to dissolve a substance. Ethanol is flammable. Suggest a safe way to heat the ethanol and explain why it is safer.
model: Use a water bath / electric heater (not a Bunsen burner).
So there is no naked flame to ignite the ethanol vapour.
exam.tip: Always explain how the precaution removes the specific hazard.

exam.q: Potassium manganate(VII) is labelled oxidising. Explain why it should be stored away from flammable substances.
model: Oxidising substances provide oxygen.
This would make a fire involving the flammable substance more intense / burn more fiercely.
exam.tip: Do not say the oxidiser itself burns.

exam.q: In the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, chlorine gas is produced at the anode. Give one hazard of this experiment and a precaution to reduce the risk.
model: Chlorine is toxic (if inhaled).
Carry out in a fume cupboard / well-ventilated room / collect only small amounts.
exam.tip: Link the precaution directly to inhaling the gas.

exam.q: A student fills a burette with sodium hydroxide solution for a titration. Give two precautions they should take and explain each.
model: Wear safety goggles.
Sodium hydroxide is corrosive/irritant and can damage eyes if splashed.
Fill the burette below eye level / remove it from the stand to fill.
So any splash or overflow cannot go into the eyes.
exam.tip: Pair each precaution with its own reason.

exam.q: Sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid, producing sulfur dioxide. Suggest why the room should be well ventilated and why extra care is needed for some students.
model: Sulfur dioxide is an irritant/harmful gas that could be inhaled; ventilation removes it.
It can trigger asthma attacks, so asthmatic students need extra care.
exam.tip: Edexcel mark schemes often credit the asthma point for this practical.

exam.q: A teacher demonstrates the reaction of sodium with water. Evaluate the hazards and describe the precautions needed.
model: Sodium reacts vigorously with water; hydrogen produced is flammable.
Corrosive sodium hydroxide solution is formed.
Use a very small piece of sodium and a large volume of water.
Use a safety screen and wear safety goggles; store sodium under oil.
exam.tip: Cover both products' hazards before the precautions.

exam.q: A student prepares copper sulfate crystals by reacting copper oxide with warm dilute sulfuric acid, filtering and then evaporating the solution. Evaluate the risks in this procedure and suggest precautions to reduce them.
model: Dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant: wear safety goggles.
Warming the acid increases the hazard: warm gently, avoid boiling, use tongs/allow to cool.
Copper oxide powder is harmful: avoid inhaling dust/skin contact, wash hands.
Copper sulfate solution is harmful and an environmental hazard: dispose of in labelled waste, not down sink.
Hot solution can spit during evaporation: stop heating before dry / heat over a water bath / evaporate slowly.
Hot apparatus can burn: use tongs or allow to cool before handling; tie back hair near Bunsen.
exam.tip: In 6-mark risk questions, work through the method step by step, giving a hazard and linked precaution at each stage.

worked.q: Write a risk assessment entry for using propanone (flammable, irritant) as the solvent in paper chromatography.
steps: Identify hazards: propanone is flammable and its vapour is an irritant.
Risk: vapour could be ignited by a Bunsen flame; vapour or liquid could irritate eyes and lungs.
Precaution 1: no naked flames in the room while the solvent is used, because there is nothing to ignite the vapour.
Precaution 2: use a small volume in a covered beaker in a well-ventilated room or fume cupboard, so less vapour is inhaled.
Precaution 3: wear safety goggles to protect eyes from splashes.
Emergency: if splashed in eyes, rinse with plenty of water and tell the teacher.
worked.ans: Propanone is flammable and irritant: keep all flames away, use a small covered volume with good ventilation and wear goggles.

worked.q: Two students both use hydrochloric acid. Student A uses 5 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 acid at room temperature. Student B uses 100 cm3 of 5 mol dm-3 acid and heats it. Compare the risks.
steps: The hazard is the same chemical, but the risk depends on concentration, quantity and temperature.
Student B's acid is 10 times more concentrated, so it is corrosive rather than just irritant: a splash causes more serious harm.
Student B uses 20 times the volume, so a spill is larger.
Heating increases the rate of damage to skin and releases hydrogen chloride fumes that can be inhaled.
So Student B's risk is much higher: they need goggles and gloves, a fume cupboard and should consider using a lower concentration.
worked.ans: Student B's procedure has a much higher risk because the acid is more concentrated, larger in volume and heated; Student A's risk is low.
